evidence_quotes.quote: In this study of Brazilian river-basin committees, the authors find that activists inside and outside the state often must collaborate to overcome resistance to change and provide state officials with resources they lack.

We then explore these questions empirically in the context of river basin committees—participatory arenas for collaboration among representatives of state agencies, associations of water users (irrigators, sanitation companies, hydroelectric firms, industries), and civic associations.
Bulk water charges on public or private entities that either extract water directly from its source or pollute rivers, lakes, or streams would be levied to finance the whole scheme.
We focus on four such committees, selected from a larger group that the Watermark Project has been studying since 2001.
In each of these cases, we found that nonstate actors sought not only to influence state decision making but also to transform state capacities to implement those decisions.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The paper examines participatory river-basin water-resource management and environmental governance (bulk raw-water extraction/pollution charges, catchment protection, coastal/land-use coordination, flood control, reforestation, and river clean-up) rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (Exclusion Criterion 7).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes plain wording, fails narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study examines legal, institutional, and governance factors—specifically state and federal water laws, participatory river-basin committees, bulk water pricing legislation, and state administrative capacity. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, it fails Criterion 2 because none of the studied mechanisms (watershed-level stakeholder deliberation, bulk water charges/permits on raw-water extractors and polluters, flood-prevention planning, and river clean-up mobilization) are rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community water/sanitation service access (such as eligibility, tenure/documentation rules, retail tariffs, disconnections, or utility service regulation). Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because Criteria 1 and 4 are not met.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Qualitative comparative case study drawing on fieldwork and interviews from the Watermark Project (Projeto Marca d'Agua) tracking Brazilian river-basin committees since 2001 across four cases (Alto Tiete, Litoral Norte, Itajai, and Velhas).
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported outcomes are institutional and watershed-governance processes—mobilization of state administrative and technical capacity, interagency coordination, flood-control and reforestation initiatives, and river pollution clean-up commitments—with no outcomes measuring household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. The unit of analysis (river-basin committee, N=4 case studies in Brazil), institutional process/exposure (state-civil society collaboration in participatory river-basin governance), outcome (state political and technical capacity to implement basin management decisions), and qualitative comparative case-study design are clearly identifiable.

population_and_sample: Four river-basin committees in Brazil (Alto Tiete and Litoral Norte in Sao Paulo, Itajai in Santa Catarina, and Velhas in Minas Gerais; unit of analysis: river-basin committee), selected from more than twenty committees studied since 2001 by the Watermark Project
exposure: Collaborations and mobilization between civil-society actors and state officials within participatory river-basin committees under Brazil's decentralized water-resource management laws
outcome: Mobilization and building of state political, administrative, and technical capacity to coordinate and implement river-basin management plans (watershed protection, flood control, reforestation, and river clean-up)
rationale: Excluded under E01 (Wrong topic; Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Although the study is an empirical qualitative comparative case study of four Brazilian river-basin committees, it investigates integrated watershed/water-resource governance (bulk raw-water pricing and permits, flood containment, reforestation, and river pollution clean-up) and state institutional capacity rather than household or community water or sanitation service access, rule-type service-access mechanisms, or household/community access outcomes.
